Computes UV coordinates for ray-Gaussian intersections to sample spatially varying colors from texture maps using bilinear interpolation.
Cast a ray from the camera origin to find intersection point $p_i$ with the i-th Gaussian.
Compute UV coordinates $u_i$ and $v_i$ using the tangent/bitangent vectors, intersection point, texel size, and texture dimensions.
Sample the texture map $T_i$ at $(u_i, v_i)$ using bilinear interpolation to obtain color $c_{tex}$.
$u_i(p_i) = \frac{(t_u)_i \cdot p_i}{T_{size}} + \frac{U_i - 1}{2}$
$v_i(p_i) = \frac{(t_v)_i \cdot p_i}{T_{size}} + \frac{V_i - 1}{2}$
A method that preserves edges better than bilinear interpolation.
Scan the low-resolution source image X to initialize a 2D array $x_{mn}$, which records the edge direction of all four-pixel squares.
Scan the high-resolution target image Y to initialize a 2D array $y_{ij}$.
Each $y_{ij}$ is inversely mapped to the sample image X.
Use the array $x_{mn}$ to identify the triangle in which the inversely mapped point falls in the source image X.
Calculate the value of $y_{ij}$ using barycentric interpolation.
Detect outliers by comparing the difference $|a - c|$ and $|b - d|$ of four pixel values (represented as heights).
The pair with the smaller difference is treated as an edge.
Comparison: Compared to bilinear interpolation, pixel level data dependent interpolation keeps edges sharp and smooth areas smooth, whereas bilinear interpolation may blur edges.
